title: 2010 AMC 12A 23
statement: The number obtained from the last two nonzero digits of \(90!\) is equal to \(n.\) What is \(n?\)

solutions.text:
The number of trailing zeroes in \(90!\) is \(\left\lfloor\dfrac{90}{5}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\dfrac{90}{25}\right\rfloor=21.\) Let \(N=\dfrac{90!}{10^{21}}.\)

There are still more than two factors of \(2\) left after removing \(10^{21},\) so \(N\equiv0 \pmod4.\)

Let \(A\) be the product of factors of \(90!\) not divisible by \(5,\) and let \(B\) be the product of the factors divisible by \(5.\) Each block \((5j+1)(5j+2)(5j+3)(5j+4)\) is \(24\equiv-1\pmod{25},\) and there are \(18\) blocks, so \(A\equiv1\pmod{25}.\)

After removing the \(21\) factors of \(5\) from \(B,\) the remaining factors can be grouped as \[ \begin{aligned} \dfrac{B}{5^{21}}={}&(1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot4) \\ &\cdot(6\cdot7\cdot8\cdot9) \\ &\cdot(11\cdot12\cdot13\cdot14) \\ &\cdot(16\cdot17\cdot18)(1\cdot2\cdot3) \\ &\equiv-1\pmod{25}. \end{aligned} \]

Therefore \(\dfrac{90!}{5^{21}}\equiv-1\pmod{25}.\) Since \(2^{21}\equiv2\pmod{25}\) and the inverse of \(2\) modulo \(25\) is \(13,\) we get \(N\equiv-13\equiv12\pmod{25}.\)

The number congruent to \(0\pmod4\) and \(12\pmod{25}\) is \(12\pmod{100},\) so the last two nonzero digits form \(12.\)

Thus, A is the correct answer.
hints: Remove the factors making trailing zeroes, then work modulo \(100\)
Use congruences modulo \(4\) and modulo \(25\) to pin down the last two digits
